text: Create Record, Update Record, and notifications all run the instant the flow reaches them — no one's permission required. Plenty of real business processes don't work that way. A new-hire equipment request shouldn't provision a laptop until a manager signs off, and a risky change shouldn't move to implementation until a change advisory board member approves it. Flow Designer's Ask for Approval actions model that real stop-and-wait behavior, instead of faking it with a Create Record and hoping someone notices.
Approval from a specific individual: one named person, often resolved through a data pill like the requester's manager, must respond, and the flow waits on that one person alone.

Approval from a group, anyone: any single member of a chosen group can approve or reject, and whichever response comes first resolves the whole step. Useful when any qualified person on a team can make the call.

Approval from a group, everyone: every member must approve before the step resolves — a single rejection, or everyone approving, closes it out. That's the right fit for a genuinely collective decision, like a multi-person change advisory board.

This isn't a cosmetic pause. An approval action creates real sysapproval_approver records — the same approval record type that drives the Approvals module elsewhere on the platform. Each approver sees it in their own approvals list, can approve or reject, and typically leaves comments explaining the decision.

The flow genuinely pauses execution at that step and only resumes once the relevant approval record reaches a final state. Because of that, you almost always follow an approval action with an If/Else condition that branches on approved versus rejected — the approval action only produces the outcome; ordinary flow logic decides what happens next.
A real pause, a real record, a real human decision. Next up: Building a Custom Reusable Action, so logic like this doesn't get duplicated across every flow that needs it.
